title: Payload Validation
description: The `raw_body` must be valid UTF-8 JSON encoding a JSON object containing: `event_id` (non-empty string, length <= 64), `type` (`"payment.captured"` or `"refund.processed"`), `payment_id` (non-empty string, length <= 64), `amount_paise` (strict JSON integer from 1 to 10^12 inclusive; not boolean, not float even if 5.0, not string, not null, not <= 0), and for `"refund.processed"` additionally `refund_id` (non-empty string). Extra unrecognized JSON fields are permitted and ignored. Any violation of these requirements: return status `"rejected"` and commit no database state change.

web.title: Validate Webhook JSON Payloads (The Right Way) | JSON Prism
web.description: Webhooks from Stripe, GitHub, and Shopify send JSON you don't control. Learn how to inspect, validate, and schema-check webhook payloads safely.
snippets: Once you know the shape you depend on, encode it as a JSON Schema and validate every incoming payload against it. A minimal schema for a payment event might require an id, an amount that's an integer, and a currency string:

Quick answer: A webhook delivers JSON your system didn't generate, so validate it before trusting it: first confirm it's syntactically valid JSON, then check it against a JSON Schema that asserts the fields and types you depend on. To inspect a captured payload by hand, paste it into the JSON Validator and explore it in the Tree View. Never assume the shape - verify it. With a webhook, an external service (Stripe, GitHub, Shopify, Slack) POSTs JSON to your endpoint when an event happens.

Schema validation catches these explicitly instead of failing deep in your code. Can I test a webhook payload without sending a request? Yes. Copy the raw body from your provider's event log and paste it into the JSON Validator to inspect and validate it locally - nothing is uploaded.

A field present in the docs' example isn't always present in every event. Types differ from expectations. An amount arrives as a string "1000" rather than a number, or a timestamp format changes. Malformed or partial bodies from retries, proxies, or truncation. If your handler reaches straight into payload.data.object.amount without checking, any of these breaks it - often silently, in production. web.title: Anatomy of a Good Webhook Payload
web.description: Learn how to design webhook payloads that developers trust: what data to include, which headers to send, how to version your schema, and the common mistakes to avoid.
snippets: Get it wrong and you'll spend months fielding tickets from frustrated engineers who can't figure out why their integrations keep breaking. This post walks through the decisions that matter when designing webhook payloads: what data to include, which headers and metadata to send alongside it, how to structure the schema for long-term sanity, and the mistakes that trip up even experienced teams. Before thinking about the event-specific data, establish a consistent wrapper that every webhook from your system will use.

A consumer that only cares about payment.succeeded shouldn't have to receive and discard hundreds of inventory.adjusted events per hour. Let consumers subscribe to specific event types. Fewer irrelevant deliveries means less wasted compute, less noise, and better security posture (you're not streaming data to endpoints that don't need it). Renaming a field from user_id to customer_id, changing an integer to a string, or restructuring nested objects — any of these will silently break consumer integrations.

A delivery ID or idempotency key (e.g., X-Webhook-Delivery-Id) gives each delivery attempt a unique identifier. This is distinct from the event ID in the body, because the same event might be delivered multiple times due to retries. Consumers use this to detect and discard duplicate deliveries. A schema version indicator — either as a header like X-Webhook-Version or embedded in the payload — tells consumers which version of the payload format they're receiving.

If you don't have a versioning strategy from day one, you'll break consumer integrations the first time you ship a schema change — and those consumers won't be gentle about it. There are a few workable approaches. Global API versioning is the simplest. Consumers subscribe at a specific version (e.g., 2026-02-01), and all webhooks they receive use that version's schema until they explicitly upgrade.
